lesson.title: Chiasmata: The X-Shaped Marks Where Chromosomes Trade Places
lesson.summary: A chiasma is the visible point where two non-sister chromatids remain physically joined after crossing over, and these connections are what hold homologous chromosomes together until they are pulled apart in anaphase I.
lesson.body:
After a crossover event finishes, the two chromatids that traded segments do not simply drift apart. They stay physically attached at the exact spot where the exchange occurred. Viewed under a microscope during late prophase I or metaphase I, this attachment point looks like an X, because it is the crossing point of two of the four chromatids in a tetrad. That X-shaped structure is called a chiasma, plural chiasmata, a name borrowed from the Greek letter chi, whose shape it resembles. A chiasma is not a separate event from crossing over. It is simply the physical, visible mark left behind by a crossover that already happened.

Chiasmata matter for more than just marking where recombination took place, though. Earlier in prophase I, the synaptonemal complex is what holds each pair of homologous chromosomes together. But that complex breaks down before metaphase I. Once it is gone, homologous chromosomes need some other way to stay paired until they are meant to separate, otherwise they could drift apart too early and be distributed randomly rather than one full homolog going to each pole. Chiasmata, together with the cohesion that still holds sister chromatids together along the rest of each chromosome, do this job. They keep the whole four-chromatid tetrad physically linked, which lets spindle fibers from opposite poles attach to each homolog and pull against that resistance, creating the tension that helps the cell correctly line up homologous pairs at the metaphase plate.

This mechanical role has real consequences. Most homologous chromosome pairs form at least one chiasma somewhere along their length during meiosis, and this is important for accurate segregation. If a pair of homologs fails to form any chiasma, there is nothing holding them together once the synaptonemal complex disassembles, and they can separate randomly or fail to separate properly, a type of error called nondisjunction that can lead to gametes with the wrong number of chromosomes. Only when the cohesin holding sister chromatids together is finally cleaved at anaphase I do the chiasmata resolve, releasing each homolog to move to opposite poles.

Taken together with the previous chapter, chiasmata are the reason crossing over is not just a fleeting molecular event. They hold the recombined chromatids in place long enough for the cell to segregate chromosomes correctly, and they are the physical evidence, visible under a microscope, that genetic recombination has taken place, which is exactly the topic of the next chapter.
